newsitem.title: UK: British unions angry at threatened new strike curb.
newsitem.headline: British unions angry at threatened new strike curb.

text.p: The British government said on Monday it was considering ways of curbing strikes after a wave of industrial unrest over the summer, but unions complained it was trying to win votes through union-bashing.
Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang told BBC radio the Conservative government's laws had already cut the strike rate to five percent of what it was at its height in the 1970s.

"What we now think is, it's time to go a little bit further, one more step, in the light of the way in which in monopoly services it is still possible for trade unions to hold the public to ransom," he said.
The summer strikes included a series of one-day stoppages by postal workers and London underground drivers. Lang refused to rule out a complete ban on strikes in such public services.
The statement caused uproar among the unions, gathered in this northern seaside town for their annual conference.
John Monks, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, told delegates the ruling Conservatives were "playing absurd politics with the lives of millions of vulnerable people".
He said they should pay more attention to the frustration and insecurity among workers that caused the strikes.
TUC officials believe the main purpose of the proposal is to spotlight the link between the unions and the opposition Labour Party in the run-up to the next election.

The unions helped found Labour and still provide almost half of its funds. Labour leader Tony Blair has cut their influence over the party but he is still worried that the union connection could be a vote-loser.
The unions were highly unpopular in the 1970s and 1980s because of widespread industrial unrest and the Conservatives pushed through a series of laws to reduce union power.

TUC officials said union-bashing would no longer win votes. According to a TUC poll published this week, 56 percent of Britons believe the Conservatives were right to introduce some reforms, but that they had gone too far.
All the same, Labour is clearly uneasy at the growth in strikes, and the fear that high expectations among unions if Labour wins power will spill over into more disputes.
Press reports have suggested Labour was planning a system of compulsory arbitration in disputes -- in effect, a ban on strikes.
But Labour employment spokesman Peter Hain told reporters on the sidelines of the conference: "We are not proposing compulsory arbitration...The right to strike will remain."
Lang poured scorn on the Labour Party's intervention.

"The difficulty they have is that they are so umbilically linked to the trade union movement that it is difficult for them to move without either damaging the national interest, if they go too close to the unions, or creating internal rows in their own party if they go in the opposite direction," he said.
